Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

issues.explanation: 'Being naked' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger for a life-threatening illness trauma unless there was a very specific exposure context; the other items point more toward nightmares/body sensations/illness-related reexperiencing, so this trigger appears poorly matched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risk-taking is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other threat and memory items describe fear, bodily alarm, pain, sensory recall, and dysregulated emotion rather than impulsive or reckless responding, so this item stands out as clinically disconnected.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: Global mistrust of other people is a weak fit with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness in the absence of any interpersonal betrayal, assault, or persecution content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the appraisals are centered on bodily threat and fear of losing control, making this item comparatively incoherent.

vignette:
Rami is a 38-year-old Middle Eastern American man who has worked for years as a hairdresser in a busy salon, where his days are structured around close attention to other people’s bodies and appearances. He lives alone and describes himself as having been independent before his illness, someone who relied on stamina, steady hands, and the ability to stay composed while clients talked to him from the chair. The event he returns to in telling his story is the period when he became seriously ill with a life-threatening medical condition and was taken into a hospital for urgent treatment. What stands out most in the way he describes it is how quickly his body stopped feeling like his own. He remembers the fear of being examined and handled while not knowing whether he would survive, the medical procedures that made him feel exposed and trapped, and the sense that danger was coming from inside him. When he talks about that time, the memory is not always visual. Sometimes what comes back first is smell: the sharp, clinical odor from the hospital and procedure rooms, vivid enough that for a moment he feels he is there again. At other times it is pain, returning in the same parts of his body that hurt during the illness, as though the memory lands physically before he has even formed a thought.

In the months afterward, Rami found that reminders arrived in ways he could not predict or control. If he came across photographs from that period—images of himself looking gaunt, pictures sent by relatives, even medical images saved on his phone—he felt his body react immediately. His chest tightened, his muscles braced, and he became flooded with fear and dread before he could look away. He began deleting and avoiding anything visual that might take him back there. Medical settings were even harder. Routine examinations that other people might treat as inconvenient felt to him like stepping back into the same threat. Sitting on an exam table, hearing the sounds of equipment, waiting for someone to touch or assess him, he became intensely tense, as if his whole body were preparing for catastrophe. He was acutely aware of strong physical reactions when reminded of the illness, and this frightened him almost as much as the reminders themselves.

Nighttime became another place where the illness returned. Rami sometimes woke from nightmares with the emotional residue still fully alive, even when he could not immediately picture what he had dreamt. He would come awake already terrified, ashamed of how shaken he was, his body rigid and alert in the dark. What unsettled him was that the feeling often arrived without a clear image, just the full force of horror and helplessness dropping into him all at once. Lying in bed afterward, he would scan himself for signs that something was wrong again. He had come to believe that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when nothing around him was unsafe, and this made rest feel unreliable.

Over time, this changed how he moved through ordinary life. At the salon, clients often wanted to show him photos on their phones—hair inspiration, family pictures, vacation snapshots—and although these were usually harmless, he had become wary of images in general. He found himself averting his eyes quickly or feeling a jolt of alarm when an unexpected hospital-related image appeared in a news feed or message notification during a quiet moment between appointments. On days when he had a medical follow-up scheduled, he was distracted at work, shoulders tight, body already preparing for the examination hours before it happened. Because hairdressing depends on calm concentration and easy conversation, this tension showed. He sometimes shortened client interactions, kept his talk superficial, or scheduled around appointments so he could leave quickly. Colleagues noticed he was more tightly wound, though he did not explain much.

The meaning he has made of these reactions is painful and frightening to him. Rami says he no longer trusts his own body. The illness taught him, in his mind, that his body can betray him without warning, and every surge of tension or physical sensation now feels like possible proof of that. When his body reacts intensely to reminders, he does not experience it as “just stress”; he takes it as evidence that something is fundamentally wrong in him. At his lowest moments, especially after waking from nightmares or leaving a medical appointment shaken, he becomes scared that these reactions mean he is going crazy. What frightens him most is not only the memory of nearly dying, but the idea that he can no longer rely on his own mind or body to tell him when he is actually safe.

He sought help after a recent medical examination left him trembling and overwhelmed for hours afterward, followed by a night in which he woke from a nightmare with the same smell and pain of the illness pressing in on him. The next day at the salon, while a client held up photos for a haircut consultation, he felt himself go rigid and had to step away to compose himself. That moment embarrassed him and made the problem harder to dismiss. Coming into treatment, he says he wants to feel that his body belongs to him again. At the same time, he is afraid that talking about what happened, or facing any reminder of it, will confirm his worst fear: that the danger never really ended, and that his body will always act as if it is about to happen again.
